vignette: A barangay health center in a rural municipality is hearing of fever with rash in one purok. Today the public health nurse sees Mia, 3 years old, who has had fever up to 39.5 C for 4 days, red watery eyes, a runny nose and a dry cough; her mother says a rash started behind the ears this morning and a cousin had the same illness last week. Mia's immunization card shows BCG, three doses of pentavalent and OPV but no measles-containing vaccine, because the family moved last year. Her mother is 5 months pregnant and cannot recall ever having measles. Mia's 7-month-old sister is with them. The waiting area is shared with other mothers and infants, and the vaccine carrier holds vials opened at 8 AM today.
stem: Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Report the suspected case to the municipal surveillance unit by phone
Give vitamin A and start a tepid sponge bath for the fever
Move Mia and her mother to a separate, well-ventilated space
Check Mia's lungs and ears for pneumonia or otitis media
optionRationales: Right action, wrong time: reporting is required but does not stop exposure of the waiting infants and the pregnant mother.
Treats the symptom: vitamin A and fever care are supportive and appropriate, but infection control comes first.
Right: separating the source breaks the chain of transmission for unvaccinated and pregnant contacts.
Skips the priority: assessing complications matters, but can be done once the child is isolated.
rationale:
1. Cues: fever, red eyes, cough and runny nose, then a rash behind the ears, no measles vaccine, and a cousin ill last week point to measles, which spreads through the air.
2. Principle: protect the susceptible people in the room (unvaccinated infants, a pregnant mother) before paperwork or comfort measures.
3. Moving Mia and her mother to a separate, ventilated space stops further exposure at once; reporting, vitamin A and fever care follow immediately after.
Flip: if Mia were already alone in a closed consultation room, notifying the municipal surveillance unit would come first.
strategy: Break the chain: isolate the source before anything else
keyFacts: Measles spreads by airborne route; airborne plus standard precautions
Pregnant women and infants are the susceptible people to protect

vignette: A barangay health center in a rural municipality is hearing of fever with rash in one purok. Today the public health nurse sees Mia, 3 years old, who has had fever up to 39.5 C for 4 days, red watery eyes, a runny nose and a dry cough; her mother says a rash started behind the ears this morning and a cousin had the same illness last week. Mia's immunization card shows BCG, three doses of pentavalent and OPV but no measles-containing vaccine, because the family moved last year. Her mother is 5 months pregnant and cannot recall ever having measles. Mia's 7-month-old sister is with them. The waiting area is shared with other mothers and infants, and the vaccine carrier holds vials opened at 8 AM today.
stem: Which actions are appropriate for the nurse's response to this suspected outbreak? Select all that apply.
options: Report the suspected cluster to the municipal health office now
Wait for laboratory confirmation before notifying anyone
Give Mia's pregnant mother measles vaccine today for protection
List contacts in the purok and check each one's immunization status
Arrange for the mother to see the physician about her exposure
Keep Mia away from infants and pregnant women while infectious
optionRationales: Right: report suspected cases promptly.
Wrong, skips action: confirmation is not needed to report and delays control.
Wrong, unsafe but common habit: the vaccine is live and is not given in pregnancy.
Right: a line list identifies susceptible contacts.
Right: non-immune pregnant exposure needs medical assessment.
Right: Mia is infectious from before the rash to about 4 days after it starts.
rationale:
1. A suspected measles cluster is reported on suspicion; waiting for laboratory confirmation delays the response.
2. A line list of contacts with their immunization status shows who is susceptible.
3. A pregnant woman who may be non-immune needs a physician's assessment, and she must not receive the live vaccine.
4. Mia is infectious from before the rash until about 4 days after it starts, so she should stay away from infants and pregnant women during that time.
Flip: if the mother were fully immunized by card, the physician referral would no longer be needed.
strategy: Notify and trace: report, line-list, protect the vulnerable
keyFacts: Live measles vaccine is not given to pregnant women
Report suspected cases without waiting for confirmation

vignette: A barangay health center in a rural municipality is hearing of fever with rash in one purok. Today the public health nurse sees Mia, 3 years old, who has had fever up to 39.5 C for 4 days, red watery eyes, a runny nose and a dry cough; her mother says a rash started behind the ears this morning and a cousin had the same illness last week. Mia's immunization card shows BCG, three doses of pentavalent and OPV but no measles-containing vaccine, because the family moved last year. Her mother is 5 months pregnant and cannot recall ever having measles. Mia's 7-month-old sister is with them. The waiting area is shared with other mothers and infants, and the vaccine carrier holds vials opened at 8 AM today.
stem: For each person identified during contact tracing, select the most appropriate action.
rows: Pregnant mother with no history of measles or vaccine
Mia, now with fast breathing and chest indrawing
columns: Refer to physician for exposure assessment
rationale: Row 1: a healthy unvaccinated 4-year-old is eligible for the live vaccine and should receive it. Row 2: the pregnant mother cannot receive the live vaccine, so she needs physician assessment. Row 3: a fully immunized, symptom-free cousin needs only teaching and watchful waiting. Row 4: fast breathing with chest indrawing suggests pneumonia, a measles complication, so urgent referral comes before anything else.
optionRationales: Right (vaccinate today): a healthy, unvaccinated child exposed in an outbreak is eligible for the live vaccine, which can still help if given early. Referring or only watching would leave the child unprotected.

Right (refer to physician): the live measles vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy, so vaccinating her is wrong. She is not sick yet, so she needs a physician to assess exposure and immunity, not just teaching.
Right (observe and teach): a fully immunized child with no symptoms is protected, so another vaccine dose or a hospital referral is unnecessary. Teaching danger signs covers the remaining risk.
Right (refer urgently): fast breathing and chest indrawing mean pneumonia, a serious measles complication. Vaccinating or only teaching delays care. Airway and breathing problems come first.
strategy: Match the action to the contact's risk
keyFacts: Live vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy
Pneumonia is a serious complication of measles

vignette: A barangay health center in a rural municipality is hearing of fever with rash in one purok. Today the public health nurse sees Mia, 3 years old, who has had fever up to 39.5 C for 4 days, red watery eyes, a runny nose and a dry cough; her mother says a rash started behind the ears this morning and a cousin had the same illness last week. Mia's immunization card shows BCG, three doses of pentavalent and OPV but no measles-containing vaccine, because the family moved last year. Her mother is 5 months pregnant and cannot recall ever having measles. Mia's 7-month-old sister is with them. The waiting area is shared with other mothers and infants, and the vaccine carrier holds vials opened at 8 AM today.
stem: The nurse explains to the staff: Measles is spread by {{1}}, a person is infectious from about {{2}}, and the type of precaution used is {{3}}.

choices: only while the rash is crusting
4 days before to 4 days after rash onset
exposure until the first day of fever
only the first day of rash

rationale: Measles travels in airborne respiratory particles, so airborne plus standard precautions are used. The infectious period runs from about 4 days before the rash until about 4 days after it appears, which is why Mia was spreading the virus before anyone knew what she had.
optionRationales: Right: measles spreads through airborne respiratory particles. Food and water, mosquito bites and blood contact are routes for other diseases (for example cholera, dengue, hepatitis B), not measles.

Right: infectiousness runs from about 4 days before to 4 days after the rash starts. The other choices are too short or start too late, which would miss the days when Mia was already spreading the virus.

Right: airborne precautions (plus standard) match the airborne mode of spread. Contact or droplet-only precautions do not stop tiny particles that stay in the air, and reverse isolation protects a vulnerable client, not others.
strategy: Chain of infection: mode of transmission decides precautions
keyFacts: Infectious about 4 days before to 4 days after rash onset
Airborne plus standard precautions

vignette: A barangay health center in a rural municipality is hearing of fever with rash in one purok. Today the public health nurse sees Mia, 3 years old, who has had fever up to 39.5 C for 4 days, red watery eyes, a runny nose and a dry cough; her mother says a rash started behind the ears this morning and a cousin had the same illness last week. Mia's immunization card shows BCG, three doses of pentavalent and OPV but no measles-containing vaccine, because the family moved last year. Her mother is 5 months pregnant and cannot recall ever having measles. Mia's 7-month-old sister is with them. The waiting area is shared with other mothers and infants, and the vaccine carrier holds vials opened at 8 AM today.
stem: Select the findings that together point to measles rather than a simple cold.
options: Fever up to 39.5 C for 4 days
Red watery eyes
Dry cough and runny nose
Rash that began behind the ears this morning
No measles-containing vaccine on the card
Mother says Mia likes to carry her doll everywhere
optionRationales: Not specific: fever occurs in many infections.
Supports: conjunctivitis is part of the pre-eruptive cluster.
Supports: cough and coryza complete the cluster.
Supports: rash behind the ears after the prodrome.
Supports: unvaccinated means susceptible.
Not relevant: her carrying a doll says nothing about measles, so it is not a diagnostic finding.
rationale: Red watery eyes plus cough and runny nose are the pre-eruptive cluster, a rash starting behind the ears after several days of fever fits the eruptive stage, and no measles-containing vaccine leaves her susceptible. A fever alone is common in colds, and the doll is irrelevant.
strategy: Pattern recognition: cluster of cues beats a single sign
keyFacts: Pre-eruptive stage: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis
Rash begins behind the ears and spreads

vignette: The public health nurse makes a home visit to Mang Tonyo, 46, a jeepney driver on day 12 of the 6-month regimen for newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis. He lives in a two-room house with his wife, who takes oral contraceptive pills, a 4-year-old grandchild with a BCG scar, and a 15-year-old son who has had a cough for three weeks. Mang Tonyo asks if the orange color of his urine means he is bleeding. He admits skipping two morning doses because he leaves at 4 AM, when his wife, who is his treatment partner, is still asleep. He swallows his tablets with breakfast. He mentions tingling in both feet for three days and says he drinks gin with co-drivers on weekends. The sleeping room has one small window.
stem: Which action is most important to prevent treatment failure and drug resistance?
options: Report the tingling in his feet so vitamin B6 can be ordered
Explain that orange urine is an expected effect of the medicine
Advise him to stop drinking gin with co-drivers
Agree on a dose time when his treatment partner can watch him swallow
optionRationales: Right action, wrong priority: B6 prevents neuropathy but does not secure cure.
True statement that does not answer the question: reassurance is needed but does not protect adherence.
Right advice, wrong priority: alcohol raises liver risk but missed doses threaten the cure.
Right: fixing the time makes observed therapy possible and prevents resistance.
rationale:
1. Cures depend on every dose being taken, observed, for six months; missed doses allow resistant bacteria to survive.
2. Orange urine is expected, the tingling is a known manageable effect, and alcohol advice matters, but none of these threatens cure as directly as missed doses.
3. Moving the observed dose to a time the treatment partner can witness fixes the cause of the missed doses.
Flip: if he had taken every dose but developed yellow eyes, reporting liver signs would be the priority.
strategy: Adherence first: DOTS prevents resistance
keyFacts: DOTS: observe each dose being swallowed
Missed doses lead to resistance

vignette: The public health nurse makes a home visit to Mang Tonyo, 46, a jeepney driver on day 12 of the 6-month regimen for newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis. He lives in a two-room house with his wife, who takes oral contraceptive pills, a 4-year-old grandchild with a BCG scar, and a 15-year-old son who has had a cough for three weeks. Mang Tonyo asks if the orange color of his urine means he is bleeding. He admits skipping two morning doses because he leaves at 4 AM, when his wife, who is his treatment partner, is still asleep. He swallows his tablets with breakfast. He mentions tingling in both feet for three days and says he drinks gin with co-drivers on weekends. The sleeping room has one small window.
stem: Which teaching points should the nurse include for Mang Tonyo and his household? Select all that apply.
options: Report numbness, yellow eyes, dark urine or vision changes
Stop the tablets once the cough has gone
Orange urine is an expected effect and not bleeding
Take the tablets with a full breakfast to protect the stomach
Avoid alcohol while on treatment
His wife should use another family planning method as well
optionRationales: Right: signals of nerve, liver or optic nerve injury.
Wrong, unsafe but common habit: stopping early causes relapse and resistance.
Right: rifampicin colors body fluids.
Wrong: food can reduce absorption of rifampicin and isoniazid.
Right: alcohol increases liver injury risk.
Right: rifampicin may reduce pill effect.
rationale: Report numbness, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine and vision changes because isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol can injure nerves, liver or optic nerve. Orange urine is expected with rifampicin. Alcohol adds liver risk. Rifampicin can make oral contraceptives less reliable, so his wife needs another method. Tablets are taken on an empty stomach for the first-line drugs, and treatment never stops because he feels better.
strategy: Teach expected effects versus reportable effects
keyFacts: Orange body fluids are expected with rifampicin
Rifampicin can reduce oral contraceptive effect

vignette: The public health nurse makes a home visit to Mang Tonyo, 46, a jeepney driver on day 12 of the 6-month regimen for newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis. He lives in a two-room house with his wife, who takes oral contraceptive pills, a 4-year-old grandchild with a BCG scar, and a 15-year-old son who has had a cough for three weeks. Mang Tonyo asks if the orange color of his urine means he is bleeding. He admits skipping two morning doses because he leaves at 4 AM, when his wife, who is his treatment partner, is still asleep. He swallows his tablets with breakfast. He mentions tingling in both feet for three days and says he drinks gin with co-drivers on weekends. The sleeping room has one small window.
stem: Match each household member or contact with the most appropriate nursing action.
rows: Neighbor who visited once, no symptoms
columns: Counsel on an additional contraceptive method
rationale: The 15-year-old has a cough of three weeks and needs evaluation now. The 4-year-old in the same house is a young close contact, so referral for evaluation is needed. The wife needs contraceptive counseling because rifampicin lowers pill reliability. A neighbor with a single brief visit and no symptoms needs only teaching and observation.
optionRationales: Right (refer now): a cough lasting three weeks in a household contact is a symptomatic case that needs sputum testing now. Waiting or only teaching would delay finding active TB.
Right (refer now): a young child in the same home is a high-risk close contact because children develop serious TB quickly. Observation alone is not enough; the child needs evaluation.
Right (counsel on another method): rifampicin speeds the breakdown of hormones, so pills may fail. She needs a back-up method. She has no TB symptoms, so TB referral is not the issue here.
Right (teach and observe): one brief visit and no symptoms means low risk. Referral for testing is not needed, but teaching about the cough sign lets the neighbor report early.
strategy: Prioritise by exposure and symptoms
keyFacts: A cough of 3 weeks or more needs TB evaluation
Young household contacts are referred for evaluation

vignette: The public health nurse makes a home visit to Mang Tonyo, 46, a jeepney driver on day 12 of the 6-month regimen for newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis. He lives in a two-room house with his wife, who takes oral contraceptive pills, a 4-year-old grandchild with a BCG scar, and a 15-year-old son who has had a cough for three weeks. Mang Tonyo asks if the orange color of his urine means he is bleeding. He admits skipping two morning doses because he leaves at 4 AM, when his wife, who is his treatment partner, is still asleep. He swallows his tablets with breakfast. He mentions tingling in both feet for three days and says he drinks gin with co-drivers on weekends. The sleeping room has one small window.
stem: The orange color of Mang Tonyo's urine is caused by {{1}}. The tingling in his feet is most likely from {{2}} and can be prevented with {{3}}.
rationale: Rifampicin colors urine and other fluids red-orange. Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy, which is prevented with vitamin B6 (pyridoxine).
optionRationales: Right: rifampicin turns urine, sweat and tears orange-red and is harmless. Isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol do not color urine this way, so naming them mixes up the side effects.
Right: isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy (tingling feet). Ethambutol affects vision, pyrazinamide raises uric acid and joint pain, and rifampicin colors fluids, so those do not fit tingling.
Right: vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) prevents isoniazid neuropathy. Vitamin C, vitamin K and folic acid are not the preventive for this drug effect.
strategy: Match drug to side effect
keyFacts: Rifampicin: red-orange fluids
Isoniazid: neuropathy, give vitamin B6

vignette: The public health nurse makes a home visit to Mang Tonyo, 46, a jeepney driver on day 12 of the 6-month regimen for newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis. He lives in a two-room house with his wife, who takes oral contraceptive pills, a 4-year-old grandchild with a BCG scar, and a 15-year-old son who has had a cough for three weeks. Mang Tonyo asks if the orange color of his urine means he is bleeding. He admits skipping two morning doses because he leaves at 4 AM, when his wife, who is his treatment partner, is still asleep. He swallows his tablets with breakfast. He mentions tingling in both feet for three days and says he drinks gin with co-drivers on weekends. The sleeping room has one small window.
stem: Select the findings that put treatment success or the client's safety at risk and need action at this visit.
options: Skipped two morning doses
Tingling in both feet
Tablets taken with breakfast
Orange urine
Weekend drinking of gin
Grandchild has a BCG scar
optionRationales: Risk: missed doses lead to resistance.
Risk: possible neuropathy needing B6.
Risk: reduced absorption.
Expected effect of rifampicin.
Risk: weekend drinking adds liver injury to the effect of the antituberculosis drugs, which can also harm the liver.
Not a risk to this treatment.
rationale: Missed doses threaten cure. Tingling signals possible isoniazid neuropathy. Taking tablets with breakfast can lower absorption of some drugs. Weekend gin adds liver risk. Orange urine is expected, and a BCG scar on the grandchild is not a risk to treatment.
strategy: Separate expected effects from true risks
keyFacts: Alcohol adds hepatotoxicity risk
Rifampicin and isoniazid are taken on an empty stomach

vignette: Ana, 29, gravida 2 para 1 at 36 weeks, was admitted with a blood pressure of 164/110 (128/84 at her last visit), a severe headache, 3+ protein on dipstick and epigastric pain. A magnesium sulfate infusion on a pump and an indwelling urinary catheter were started 4 hours ago. At the 0400 check her respiratory rate is 10/min, her patellar reflexes are absent, urine output over the last hour is 20 mL, blood pressure is 150/100 and the fetal heart rate is 140/min with moderate variability. Her husband asks if he can turn the television on for her. The room lights are bright, and the nurse knows that a suction set-up is at the bedside and calcium gluconate is in the medication room.
stem: What should the nurse do first?
options: Draw a magnesium level and wait for the result before changing anything
Apply oxygen by mask and recheck her respirations in 15 minutes
Stop the magnesium infusion and call the provider
Give the PRN antihypertensive ordered for severe-range blood pressure
optionRationales: Under-reaction: a level is useful but the clinical signs already demand action.
Treats the symptom: oxygen helps breathing but the drug keeps infusing.
Right: stop the cause, then support breathing and obtain the antidote order.
Over-looks the cause: blood pressure is improving and is not the immediate threat.
rationale:
1. Respiratory rate under about 12, absent reflexes and low urine output are the three signs of magnesium toxicity, and magnesium is cleared by the kidneys, so toxicity can keep rising.
2. Priority rule: stop the cause, then support breathing, then notify and prepare the antidote.
3. Oxygen alone or a level draw leaves the drug running.
Flip: if respirations were 18 and only the reflexes were brisk, the infusion would continue with closer monitoring.
strategy: Remove the cause first: stop the drug
keyFacts: Check reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output before each dose
Calcium gluconate is the antidote

vignette: Ana, 29, gravida 2 para 1 at 36 weeks, was admitted with a blood pressure of 164/110 (128/84 at her last visit), a severe headache, 3+ protein on dipstick and epigastric pain. A magnesium sulfate infusion on a pump and an indwelling urinary catheter were started 4 hours ago. At the 0400 check her respiratory rate is 10/min, her patellar reflexes are absent, urine output over the last hour is 20 mL, blood pressure is 150/100 and the fetal heart rate is 140/min with moderate variability. Her husband asks if he can turn the television on for her. The room lights are bright, and the nurse knows that a suction set-up is at the bedside and calcium gluconate is in the medication room.
stem: Hours later, the nurse finds Ana in a tonic-clonic seizure, lying on her back. What should the nurse do first?
options: Insert a padded airway between her teeth
Turn her to her side and protect her head
Press the call bell and go to the medication room
Give the ordered extra magnesium bolus right away
optionRationales: Unsafe but common habit: objects in the mouth cause injury and obstruction.
Right: side-lying protects the airway and prevents injury.
Right action, wrong time: she must not be left, and airway comes first.
Treats the symptom while the airway is unprotected; drug comes after airway and safety.
rationale:
Turning her to her side drains saliva and protects the airway, which comes before medication or phone calls. Nothing goes in the mouth; suction is used if needed. After the seizure, give oxygen, assess, check the fetal heart and then give ordered drugs.
Flip: if she were already on her side with a clear airway, getting help would become the first act.
strategy: ABC and safety during seizure
keyFacts: During a seizure nothing in the mouth; turn to side
Airway first, then safety, then medication

vignette: Ana, 29, gravida 2 para 1 at 36 weeks, was admitted with a blood pressure of 164/110 (128/84 at her last visit), a severe headache, 3+ protein on dipstick and epigastric pain. A magnesium sulfate infusion on a pump and an indwelling urinary catheter were started 4 hours ago. At the 0400 check her respiratory rate is 10/min, her patellar reflexes are absent, urine output over the last hour is 20 mL, blood pressure is 150/100 and the fetal heart rate is 140/min with moderate variability. Her husband asks if he can turn the television on for her. The room lights are bright, and the nurse knows that a suction set-up is at the bedside and calcium gluconate is in the medication room.
stem: Classify each finding.
rows: Warm, flushed feeling when the infusion starts
rationale: Warmth and flushing are common at the start of magnesium infusion. Absent reflexes and a respiratory rate of 10 signal toxicity. New right-upper-quadrant pain with preeclampsia points to worsening disease such as HELLP and must be reported.
optionRationales: Right (expected effect): warmth and flushing are common when magnesium infusion starts and are not harmful on their own. Calling this toxicity or worsening disease would cause needless alarm.

Right (magnesium toxicity): absent patellar reflexes are the early warning of too much magnesium, so the infusion is held and the provider told. It is not an expected effect, and it is not a disease sign.
Right (worsening disease): new right upper quadrant pain in preeclampsia suggests liver involvement such as HELLP. It is not caused by magnesium and is not harmless, so report it.

Right (magnesium toxicity): a respiratory rate of 10 per minute means respiratory depression from magnesium. Breathing is a priority, so stop the infusion and call for help. It is not an expected effect.
strategy: Recognise toxicity versus expected effect versus worsening disease
keyFacts: Absent reflexes and respiratory rate under 12 signal toxicity
Epigastric or RUQ pain signals worsening disease

vignette: Ana, 29, gravida 2 para 1 at 36 weeks, was admitted with a blood pressure of 164/110 (128/84 at her last visit), a severe headache, 3+ protein on dipstick and epigastric pain. A magnesium sulfate infusion on a pump and an indwelling urinary catheter were started 4 hours ago. At the 0400 check her respiratory rate is 10/min, her patellar reflexes are absent, urine output over the last hour is 20 mL, blood pressure is 150/100 and the fetal heart rate is 140/min with moderate variability. Her husband asks if he can turn the television on for her. The room lights are bright, and the nurse knows that a suction set-up is at the bedside and calcium gluconate is in the medication room.
stem: The antidote for magnesium toxicity is {{1}}, and because magnesium is cleared by the {{2}}, low urine output {{3}} the risk of toxicity.
rationale: Calcium gluconate reverses magnesium effects. Magnesium leaves the body through the kidneys, so oliguria allows levels to rise.
optionRationales: Right: calcium gluconate is the antidote that reverses magnesium effects. Protamine reverses heparin, vitamin K reverses warfarin and naloxone reverses opioids.
Right: magnesium leaves the body through the kidneys. The liver, lungs and bile are not the main route, so they do not explain the link to urine output.
Right: low urine output raises the risk because magnesium is retained. Saying it lowers or does not change the risk ignores that the kidneys clear the drug, which is why urine output is checked.
strategy: Know the antidote and why urine output matters
keyFacts: Calcium gluconate at the bedside
Urine output at least about 30 mL/hour

vignette: Ana, 29, gravida 2 para 1 at 36 weeks, was admitted with a blood pressure of 164/110 (128/84 at her last visit), a severe headache, 3+ protein on dipstick and epigastric pain. A magnesium sulfate infusion on a pump and an indwelling urinary catheter were started 4 hours ago. At the 0400 check her respiratory rate is 10/min, her patellar reflexes are absent, urine output over the last hour is 20 mL, blood pressure is 150/100 and the fetal heart rate is 140/min with moderate variability. Her husband asks if he can turn the television on for her. The room lights are bright, and the nurse knows that a suction set-up is at the bedside and calcium gluconate is in the medication room.
stem: Select the findings at the 0400 check that mean the infusion must be held.
options: Respiratory rate 10/min
Patellar reflexes absent
Urine output 20 mL in the last hour
Blood pressure 150/100
Fetal heart rate 140/min with moderate variability
Husband asking about television
optionRationales: Hold sign: a respiratory rate of 10 per minute shows magnesium toxicity is depressing breathing, so the infusion is held.
Hold sign: absent patellar reflexes are an early sign of magnesium toxicity, so the infusion is held.
Hold sign: kidneys clear magnesium.
Improving, expected.
Not a hold sign: a fetal heart rate of 140 with moderate variability is reassuring and gives no reason to stop the infusion.
Irrelevant to hold decision.
rationale: Respiratory rate 10, absent reflexes and low urine output are hold signs. A falling blood pressure and a reassuring fetal heart rate are not reasons to hold, and the husband's request is a comfort question.
strategy: Hold criteria versus reassuring data
keyFacts: Hold for respiratory rate under 12, absent reflexes, low urine output

vignette: Baby Rico, 8 months, has tetralogy of Fallot and is waiting for surgery. His mother brings him to the district hospital emergency room after 2 days of diarrhea and poor feeding. He has been crying inconsolably since morning and is now deeply blue, limp and breathing fast and deeply. His pulse oximeter reads 68%. The fontanelle is sunken, there are no tears, and the mother is holding him upright against her shoulder. No intravenous line is in place.
stem: Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Start an intravenous line for fluid replacement
Place him in a knee-chest position with oxygen, keeping him calm
Give oral rehydration solution by cup
Take a blood sample for electrolytes
optionRationales: Right action, wrong time: needed soon but agitating him first worsens the spell.
Right: position and oxygen reverse the shunt while he is kept calm.
Treats the cause late: feeding a cyanotic infant who is breathing hard risks aspiration.
Skips the priority: labs can wait until he is stable.
rationale:
1. Dehydration thickens blood and crying raises oxygen demand, triggering a hypercyanotic spell.
2. Knee-chest or side-lying with knees up raises systemic vascular resistance and sends more blood to the lungs, and oxygen and calm follow at once.
3. Fluids are needed, but starting an IV on a screaming blue infant first worsens the spell.
Flip: if the baby were pink and only dehydrated, IV or oral rehydration would be first.
strategy: ABC with a physiologic fix: position first
keyFacts: Tet spell: knee-chest position, oxygen, keep calm
Position raises systemic resistance and lung blood flow

vignette: Baby Rico, 8 months, has tetralogy of Fallot and is waiting for surgery. His mother brings him to the district hospital emergency room after 2 days of diarrhea and poor feeding. He has been crying inconsolably since morning and is now deeply blue, limp and breathing fast and deeply. His pulse oximeter reads 68%. The fontanelle is sunken, there are no tears, and the mother is holding him upright against her shoulder. No intravenous line is in place.
stem: After he recovers, which nursing plan best reduces the chance of another spell?
options: Restrict fluids to reduce the workload on the heart
Wake him on a fixed schedule for routine vital signs
Cluster care and keep him calm and well hydrated
Keep him lying flat on his back for most of the day
optionRationales: Unsafe: dehydration thickens blood and can trigger a spell.
Over-intervention: waking a calm infant increases crying.
Right: removes the common triggers.
Plausible detail from another condition; flat positioning does not prevent spells.
rationale: Crying, dehydration, fever and straining raise oxygen demand and thicken blood. Planning calm, clustered care and maintaining hydration reduces triggers. Restricting fluids or waking him for routine care adds triggers.
strategy: Prevent the trigger
keyFacts: Triggers: crying, dehydration, feeding exertion

vignette: Baby Rico, 8 months, has tetralogy of Fallot and is waiting for surgery. His mother brings him to the district hospital emergency room after 2 days of diarrhea and poor feeding. He has been crying inconsolably since morning and is now deeply blue, limp and breathing fast and deeply. His pulse oximeter reads 68%. The fontanelle is sunken, there are no tears, and the mother is holding him upright against her shoulder. No intravenous line is in place.
stem: The mother asks about other heart defects. Classify each as cyanotic or acyanotic.
rationale: Tetralogy of Fallot, transposition of the great vessels and tricuspid atresia send unoxygenated blood to the body (cyanotic). Atrial septal defect is typically acyanotic because flow is left to right.
optionRationales: Right (cyanotic): Tetralogy of Fallot includes pulmonary stenosis and a right-to-left shunt, so unoxygenated blood reaches the body.
Right (acyanotic): in atrial septal defect the shunt is left to right, so oxygenated blood recirculates and there is no cyanosis early on.
Right (cyanotic): in transposition the two circuits run in parallel, so oxygen-poor blood goes to the body. Survival depends on a mixing defect.
Right (acyanotic): patent ductus arteriosus shunts blood left to right, from the aorta to the pulmonary artery, so it is acyanotic.
strategy: Right-to-left shunt means cyanosis
keyFacts: Cyanotic: tetralogy, truncus, tricuspid atresia, transposition

vignette: Baby Rico, 8 months, has tetralogy of Fallot and is waiting for surgery. His mother brings him to the district hospital emergency room after 2 days of diarrhea and poor feeding. He has been crying inconsolably since morning and is now deeply blue, limp and breathing fast and deeply. His pulse oximeter reads 68%. The fontanelle is sunken, there are no tears, and the mother is holding him upright against her shoulder. No intravenous line is in place.
stem: The knee-chest position {{1}} systemic vascular resistance, which {{2}} blood flow to the lungs.
rationale: Flexing the legs raises systemic vascular resistance, which shifts more blood through the lungs instead of across the septal defect.
optionRationales: Right: flexing the legs (knee-chest) raises systemic vascular resistance. Lowering would defeat the purpose of the position.
Right: higher systemic resistance pushes more blood toward the lungs instead of across the defect, so lung blood flow increases. A decrease would mean the position does not help the cyanotic spell.
strategy: Understand the why of the position
keyFacts: Knee-chest raises systemic resistance

stem: Select the factors that most likely triggered today's spell.

Inconsolable crying since morning

optionRationales: Dehydration thickens blood.
Raises oxygen demand.

rationale: Diarrhea with dehydration, inconsolable crying and poor feeding explain a rise in oxygen demand and thicker blood. Being held upright and the underlying defect do not by themselves trigger today's spell.
strategy: Identify the trigger among the cues
keyFacts: Triggers: crying, dehydration
